ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants completed the experiment independently on a desktop or laptop computer at a time and location of their choosing and were instructed to perform the task alone in a quiet environment.
All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the experiment and were informed that participation was restricted to individuals aged 16-35 years.
In Experiment 1, written informed consent was obtained using pen and paper before the testing session.
In Experiment 2, participants provided electronic informed consent by selecting an "I agree" option before beginning the online experiment.
A total of 57 participants were recruited through the Ghent University SONA participant pool and received one course credit per hour of participation.
Two participants were excluded because they did not meet the learning criteria described in the Exclusion criteria section, resulting in a final sample of 54 participants.
Participants were aged 17-25 years (M = 18.70, SD = 1.37; female = 40).
A separate sample of 78 participants was recruited through the Ghent University SONA participant pool and received one course credit per hour of participation.
Eleven participants were excluded because they did not meet the learning criteria, resulting in a final sample of 67 participants.
Participants were aged 18-32 years (M = 19.75, SD = 2.34; female = 41).

After providing informed consent and demographic information, participants completed eight phases in a fixed order (see Fig. 1a): (1) food selection, (2) pressing-capacity calibration, (3) baseline food ratings, (4) instrumental effort training, ( 5 responded to questions to make sure they understood the instructions.

table.text: Participants were required to move the slider before the continue button became available, preventing trials from being completed without an active response.

Following previous physical-effort paradigms in which effort requirements were individually calibrated (Arulpragasam et al., 2018; Gabay et al., 2024; Seaman et al., 2018), participants completed a pressing-capacity calibration to account for individual differences in motor response capacity.

table.text: Participants completed 12 maximum pressing capacity (MPC) trials: six using the A key with the left index finger and six using the L key with the right index finger.
Participants were instructed to press the indicated key as many times as possible for 6 seconds.
A red fixation cross appeared, and participants were required to press the space bar to continue.
At the end of each block, participants completed five selfpaced contingency questions assessing knowledge of the cue-outcome associations.
All participants completed all three Pavlovian-training blocks; progression through training did not depend on contingencyquestion accuracy.
Participants were free to respond using the A key, the L key, or to alternate between the two responses; simultaneous keypresses were not permitted.

Participants were nevertheless instructed that their responses could still earn food rewards and no actual food reward in the current studies, such that transfer was assessed under nominal extinction, consistent with common procedures in human PIT research (Badioli et al., 2024; Finotti et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026).

table.text: Following the transfer test, participants completed three questions concerning their response strategy and subjective experience during transfer.
For instrumental learning, participants were required to achieve at least 50% response-side accuracy in their final completed training block.

For Pavlovian learning, participants were excluded if attention-check accuracy was below 50%, mean attention-check response time exceeded 5,000 ms, or cue-outcome contingency accuracy was below 50% in the final training block.
Sensitivity analyses restricted to these participants are summarised in Section 3.8 and reported fully in Supplementary Results S2.
Eight participants completed instrumental training after two blocks, whereas 46 completed a third block.

table.text: Participants were more likely than chance to select the outcome-congruent action first under both low-and high-effort cues, but effort history did not alter the probability of making that congruent first choice in either experiment.
The slider was initially positioned at the midpoint of the scale, and participants were required to move it before continuing.
Participants had up to 12 s from presentation of the response display to initiate responding; failure to do so resulted in "Too slow" feedback.

Trials on which the effort threshold was not reached produced no food outcome and did not contribute to the block-completion criterion: the block ended when participants had obtained nine rewarded outcomes in each of the four response-effort conditions.

Because reward delivery was probabilistic and unsuccessful trials did not contribute to this criterion, the number of trials required to complete a block varied across participants.At the end of each block, participants completed eight contingency questions assessing knowledge of the instrumental contingencies.
Participants completed a minimum of two and a maximum of three training blocks.
Training ended once participants had completed two consecutive correct blocks, or after completion of the third block regardless of whether the criterion had been reached.

> All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the experiment and were informed that participation was restricted to individuals aged 16-35 years.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power (Version 3.1.9.6; Faul et al., 2009) for the critical Response × Cue interaction in a 2 × 5 repeated-measures ANOVA.

Assuming an effect size of f = 0.20, an alpha level of 0.05, 80% power, a correlation of 0.50 among repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 0.75, the analysis indicated a minimum required sample of 38 participants. The Response × Cue interaction was selected because the primary outcome-specific transfer hypothesis concerned whether Pavlovian cue identity differentially biased response allocation between the left and right instrumental actions.

In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≥ 0.110", Text = "Importantly, neither the main effect of Outcome nor the Time × Outcome interaction was significant for any rating dimension in either experiment (all ps ≥ 0.110)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 123 columns across 12 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants completed the experiment independently on a desktop or laptop computer at a time and location of their choosing and were instructed to perform the task alone in a quiet environment.
All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the experiment and were informed that participation was restricted to individuals aged 16-35 years.
In Experiment 1, written informed consent was obtained using pen and paper before the testing session.
In Experiment 2, participants provided electronic informed consent by selecting an "I agree" option before beginning the online experiment.
A total of 57 participants were recruited through the Ghent University SONA participant pool and received one course credit per hour of participation.
Two participants were excluded because they did not meet the learning criteria described in the Exclusion criteria section, resulting in a final sample of 54 participants.
Participants were aged 17-25 years (M = 18.70, SD = 1.37; female = 40).
A separate sample of 78 participants was recruited through the Ghent University SONA participant pool and received one course credit per hour of participation.
Eleven participants were excluded because they did not meet the learning criteria, resulting in a final sample of 67 participants.
Participants were aged 18-32 years (M = 19.75, SD = 2.34; female = 41).

After providing informed consent and demographic information, participants completed eight phases in a fixed order (see Fig. 1a): (1) food selection, (2) pressing-capacity calibration, (3) baseline food ratings, (4) instrumental effort training, ( 5 responded to questions to make sure they understood the instructions.
Participants were required to move the slider before the continue button became available, preventing trials from being completed without an active response.

Following previous physical-effort paradigms in which effort requirements were individually calibrated (Arulpragasam et al., 2018; Gabay et al., 2024; Seaman et al., 2018), participants completed a pressing-capacity calibration to account for individual differences in motor response capacity.
Participants completed 12 maximum pressing capacity (MPC) trials: six using the A key with the left index finger and six using the L key with the right index finger.
Participants were instructed to press the indicated key as many times as possible for 6 seconds.
A red fixation cross appeared, and participants were required to press the space bar to continue.
At the end of each block, participants completed five selfpaced contingency questions assessing knowledge of the cue-outcome associations.
All participants completed all three Pavlovian-training blocks; progression through training did not depend on contingencyquestion accuracy.
Participants were free to respond using the A key, the L key, or to alternate between the two responses; simultaneous keypresses were not permitted.

Participants were nevertheless instructed that their responses could still earn food rewards and no actual food reward in the current studies, such that transfer was assessed under nominal extinction, consistent with common procedures in human PIT research (Badioli et al., 2024; Finotti et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026).
Following the transfer test, participants completed three questions concerning their response strategy and subjective experience during transfer.
For instrumental learning, participants were required to achieve at least 50% response-side accuracy in their final completed training block.

For Pavlovian learning, participants were excluded if attention-check accuracy was below 50%, mean attention-check response time exceeded 5,000 ms, or cue-outcome contingency accuracy was below 50% in the final training block.
Sensitivity analyses restricted to these participants are summarised in Section 3.8 and reported fully in Supplementary Results S2.
Eight participants completed instrumental training after two blocks, whereas 46 completed a third block.
Four participants completed training after two blocks, whereas 63 completed a third block.

Participants were more likely than chance to select the outcome-congruent action first under both low-and high-effort cues, but effort history did not alter the probability of making that congruent first choice in either experiment.
The slider was initially positioned at the midpoint of the scale, and participants were required to move it before continuing.
Participants had up to 12 s from presentation of the response display to initiate responding; failure to do so resulted in "Too slow" feedback.

Trials on which the effort threshold was not reached produced no food outcome and did not contribute to the block-completion criterion: the block ended when participants had obtained nine rewarded outcomes in each of the four response-effort conditions.

Because reward delivery was probabilistic and unsuccessful trials did not contribute to this criterion, the number of trials required to complete a block varied across participants.At the end of each block, participants completed eight contingency questions assessing knowledge of the instrumental contingencies.
Participants completed a minimum of two and a maximum of three training blocks.
Training ended once participants had completed two consecutive correct blocks, or after completion of the third block regardless of whether the criterion had been reached.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("01_control_analysis_script.Rmd", 
"02_transfer_analysis_script.Rmd", "03_subjective_effort_sensitivity_script.Rmd"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "01_control_analysis_script.Rmd", 
"01_control_analysis_script.Rmd"), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", 
"dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Missing inputs
4 input files the code reads are in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("anova_mpc_long.rds", "anova_instrumental_long.rds", 
"anova_reward_rating_t0_t1_long.rds", "anova_pavlovian_long.rds"
), Status = c("absent", "absent", "absent", "absent"), Reason = c("the deposit holds anova_mpc_long.csv, the code reads anova_mpc_long.rds", 
"the deposit holds anova_instrumental_long.csv, the code reads anova_instrumental_long.rds", 
"the deposit holds anova_reward_rating_t0_t1_long.csv, the code reads anova_reward_rating_t0_t1_long.rds", 
"the deposit holds anova_pavlovian_long.csv, the code reads anova_pavlovian_long.rds"
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 6 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `anova_pavlovian_wide.rds`, `p4_clean.rds`, `p4_trials.rds`, `p5_clean.rds`, `demographics_clean.rds`, `p7_clean.rds`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

), "Time (s)" = c(3.5, 3.5, 3.4)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)

info.title: When Effort Invigorates: Instrumental Effort History Increases Cue-Evoked Response Vigour While Preserving Outcome-Specific Transfer

text.text: Environmental cues can influence action through outcome-related information learned elsewhere, but whether features of the instrumental acquisition history associated with those outcomes remain behaviourally relevant when the outcomes are later predicted by Pavlovian cues is unknown.

Across two experiments, one conducted in the laboratory (N = 54) and one online (N = 67), we separated instrumental acquisition under low-and high-effort response requirements from Pavlovian cue learning.
Participants first learned that different actions produced outcomes under relatively low or high effort requirements and separately learned cues predicting those same outcomes.
Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT) was then tested under extinction, with neither outcomes nor response requirements present.
In both experiments, reward-predictive cues elicited greater response vigour than a control cue.
Critically, cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under high-effort response requirements elicited greater responding than cues predicting outcomes obtained under low-effort requirements.
Specific PIT was robust under both acquisition conditions, with cues selectively promoting actions associated with their predicted outcomes.

There was also suggestive evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified the magnitude of specific PIT, but this modulation was not consistently supported across experiments or statistical approaches.
No corresponding effect emerged for initial outcome-congruent action selection.

Overall, response vigour was modulated by instrumental effort history more consistently than outcome-specific action selection, indicating that features of prior effortful instrumental experience can remain behaviourally relevant when the associated outcomes are later predicted by separately learned Pavlovian cues.
Goal pursuit often requires effort.
Obtaining food, completing work, exercising, and pursuing long-term goals all require individuals to invest physical or cognitive resources in the service of desired outcomes.

Effort therefore plays a central role in motivation, shaping both whether an action is worth pursuing and how much behavioural investment is mobilised to obtain its consequence (Salamone & Correa, 2024).
text.formatted: Effort therefore plays a central role in motivation, shaping both whether an action is worth pursuing and how much behavioural investment is mobilised to obtain its consequence <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Salamone & Correa, 2024</ref>).

text.text: Yet the consequences of effort are not straightforward.

Although anticipated effort is commonly treated as a cost that discourages action, accumulating evidence suggests that effort already invested can continue to influence subsequent evaluation, learning, and behaviour (Inzlicht et al., 2018; Jarvis et al., 2022; Stähler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Although anticipated effort is commonly treated as a cost that discourages action, accumulating evidence suggests that effort already invested can continue to influence subsequent evaluation, learning, and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jarvis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Stähler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a broader question: does the history of how an outcome was obtained continue to influence behaviour even after the original effort requirement is no longer present?
Much of the effort literature conceptualizes effort prospectively as a cost.

When more effort is required to obtain an otherwise equivalent reward, individuals are generally less willing to pursue it, a phenomenon commonly described as effort discounting (Białaszek et al., 2017; Chong et al., 2017; Escobar & Mitchell, 2025).
text.formatted: When more effort is required to obtain an otherwise equivalent reward, individuals are generally less willing to pursue it, a phenomenon commonly described as effort discounting <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Białaszek et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Escobar & Mitchell, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Effort allocation, however, depends not only on objective response demand but also on expected reward, task difficulty, perceived attainability, and the expected benefit of further investment (Silvestrini et al., 2023; Vassena et al., 2019; Verguts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Effort allocation, however, depends not only on objective response demand but also on expected reward, task difficulty, perceived attainability, and the expected benefit of further investment <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Silvestrini et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Vassena et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verguts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Reward and effort information may also be weighted differently depending on current task demands rather than being combined into a fixed scalar value (Vassena et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Reward and effort information may also be weighted differently depending on current task demands rather than being combined into a fixed scalar value <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Vassena et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Effort is therefore better understood as an action cost whose motivational impact depends on both anticipated demand and the context in which behavioural investment is evaluated.
In line with this conceptualization of anticipated effort as a cost, exerting (physical) effort can impose negative consequences for subsequent performance.

For instance, repetitive finger movements can induce central motor fatigue (Arias et al., 2015), increase perceived fatigue (Soto-Leon et al., 2020), and, under high response requirements, produce slower responding (Bowyer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For instance, repetitive finger movements can induce central motor fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arias et al., 2015)</ref>, increase perceived fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Soto-Leon et al., 2020)</ref>, and, under high response requirements, produce slower responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bowyer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accumulating fatigue can in turn influence subsequent motivation and effort-based choice (Matthews et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Accumulating fatigue can in turn influence subsequent motivation and effort-based choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Matthews et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, greater prior effort exertion might therefore be expected to suppress rather than promote later responding.
The consequences of completed effort, however, do not always mirror those of anticipated effort.

The effort paradox describes how effort is generally avoided prospectively but can, under some conditions, enhance the value of its consequences or increase later willingness to engage in demanding behaviour (Inzlicht et al., 2018; Clay et al., 2022; Job et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The effort paradox describes how effort is generally avoided prospectively but can, under some conditions, enhance the value of its consequences or increase later willingness to engage in demanding behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Clay et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Job et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, rewarding cognitive effort can increase subsequent preference for demanding activities even when the external reward is no longer available (Clay et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, rewarding cognitive effort can increase subsequent preference for demanding activities even when the external reward is no longer available <ref type="bibr">(Clay et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Greater physical effort can decrease outcome value when considered prospectively yet increase it when evaluated retrospectively (Marcowski et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Greater physical effort can decrease outcome value when considered prospectively yet increase it when evaluated retrospectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Marcowski et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Electrophysiological evidence further suggests that prior physical effort modulates neural responses during reward-outcome evaluation, with reduced reward positivity (RewP) during early feedback processing but enhanced late positive potential (LPP) during later processing (Wu & Zheng, 2023).
text.formatted: Electrophysiological evidence further suggests that prior physical effort modulates neural responses during reward-outcome evaluation, with reduced reward positivity (RewP) during early feedback processing but enhanced late positive potential (LPP) during later processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Wu & Zheng, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These effects also depend on how effort is experienced: greater effort can enhance subsequent reward valuation when individuals perceive their actions as contributing to the outcome, whereas the opposite pattern can occur when perceived control is low (Harmon-Jones et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These effects also depend on how effort is experienced: greater effort can enhance subsequent reward valuation when individuals perceive their actions as contributing to the outcome, whereas the opposite pattern can occur when perceived control is low <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Harmon-Jones et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, recent accounts propose that the value assigned to effort depends on its perceived instrumentality for attaining valued goals rather than on effort being intrinsically costly or rewarding in a uniform way (Job et al., 2024).
text.formatted: More broadly, recent accounts propose that the value assigned to effort depends on its perceived instrumentality for attaining valued goals rather than on effort being intrinsically costly or rewarding in a uniform way <ref type="bibr">(Job et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Completed effort therefore does not uniformly increase or decrease outcome value.
Learning perspectives further suggest that these effort-based modulations can persist beyond the initial context in which the action was performed and evaluated. .

Stimuli associated with greater preceding physical effort can subsequently acquire greater preference even when the effortful actions themselves remain less attractive (Alessandri et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Stimuli associated with greater preceding physical effort can subsequently acquire greater preference even when the effortful actions themselves remain less attractive <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alessandri et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Klein et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Learned-industriousness theory similarly proposes that reinforcement of high effort can condition value to effort-related experience and thereby promote subsequent persistence (Eisenberger, 1992).
text.formatted: Learned-industriousness theory similarly proposes that reinforcement of high effort can condition value to effort-related experience and thereby promote subsequent persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Eisenberger, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: More directly, Jarvis et al. (2022) showed that physical effort altered reinforcement learning, strengthening learning from positive outcomes while attenuating learning from negative outcomes.
text.formatted: More directly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jarvis et al. (2022)</ref> showed that physical effort altered reinforcement learning, strengthening learning from positive outcomes while attenuating learning from negative outcomes.

text.text: Together, effort requirements can therefore influence not only whether and how an action is undertaken but also how this implementation is evaluated and how it influences learning and subsequent behaviour.
A complementary question concerns how information about effort requirements is acquired in the first place.

In everyday behaviour, individuals are rarely given precise information about how demanding an action will be and must instead learn this through experience. Skvortsova et al. (2014) showed that expected physical effort can be updated through prediction errors, supported by neural systems partly distinct from those involved in reward learning. Hauser et al. (2017) similarly identified parallel effort-and reward-prediction-error signals that were subsequently integrated during action evaluation.
text.formatted: In everyday behaviour, individuals are rarely given precise information about how demanding an action will be and must instead learn this through experience. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Skvortsova et al. (2014)</ref> showed that expected physical effort can be updated through prediction errors, supported by neural systems partly distinct from those involved in reward learning. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hauser et al. (2017)</ref> similarly identified parallel effort-and reward-prediction-error signals that were subsequently integrated during action evaluation.

text.text: Adaptive-effort accounts further propose that individuals learn when additional investment is worthwhile from the relationship between effort, reward, and task performance (Otto et al., 2022; Verguts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Adaptive-effort accounts further propose that individuals learn when additional investment is worthwhile from the relationship between effort, reward, and task performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Otto et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verguts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work by Bi et al. (2026) extends this account by showing that learned expectations about required physical effort are combined with ongoing sensorimotor feedback and updated as environmental conditions change.
text.formatted: Recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bi et al. (2026)</ref> extends this account by showing that learned expectations about required physical effort are combined with ongoing sensorimotor feedback and updated as environmental conditions change.

text.text: Effort expectations are therefore learned and dynamically updated rather than fixed properties of an action.

Together, these findings establish two complementary principles: effort requirements can be learned from instrumental experience, and prior completed effort can alter subsequent learning and evaluation.

A broader theoretical question is whether such effects remain tied to the action through which effort was experienced or become incorporated into representations of the associated outcome and can therefore influence behaviour in a different context.

This distinction is important because these alternatives imply different mechanisms: an action-bound effect would reflect learning specific to the effortful response, whereas transfer beyond the original action context would suggest that some feature of effort history is retrieved through the associated outcome.
Addressing this question requires separating the later expression of behaviour from the action through which effort was originally experienced.
Otherwise, any difference could reflect current response demand, residual fatigue, motor repetition, or direct learning about the effortful action itself.
Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer provides a way to make this separation.
In Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT), instrumental response-outcome and Pavlovian cue-outcome relations are learned separately.

During transfer, Pavlovian cues can nevertheless influence instrumental responding despite never having been directly paired with the instrumental actions, typically under extinction so that newly delivered outcomes cannot shape behaviour during the test (Badioli et al., 2024; Cartoni et al., 2016).
text.formatted: During transfer, Pavlovian cues can nevertheless influence instrumental responding despite never having been directly paired with the instrumental actions, typically under extinction so that newly delivered outcomes cannot shape behaviour during the test <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Badioli et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cartoni et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: PIT can be expressed in different aspects of instrumental behaviour.

Specific PIT reflects outcome-specific action selection: a cue predicting a particular outcome preferentially promotes the action that previously produced that same outcome (Cartoni et al., 2016; Sennwald et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Specific PIT reflects outcome-specific action selection: a cue predicting a particular outcome preferentially promotes the action that previously produced that same outcome <ref type="bibr">(Cartoni et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Sennwald et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: General PIT is more closely associated with response invigoration, whereby reward-predictive cues increase overall instrumental activity (da Costa et al., 2020; Talmi et al., 2008).
text.formatted: General PIT is more closely associated with response invigoration, whereby reward-predictive cues increase overall instrumental activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(da Costa et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Talmi et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, these effects map onto two distinguishable dimensions of motivated behaviour: which action is selected and how vigorously behaviour is expressed (Salamone & Correa, 2012 , 2024).
text.formatted: More broadly, these effects map onto two distinguishable dimensions of motivated behaviour: which action is selected and how vigorously behaviour is expressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Salamone & Correa, 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This mapping is not absolute: outcome-specific cues can also alter overall responding, and ostensibly general transfer can retain sensitivity to broader outcome properties (Mahlberg & Weidemann, 2024).
text.formatted: This mapping is not absolute: outcome-specific cues can also alter overall responding, and ostensibly general transfer can retain sensitivity to broader outcome properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mahlberg & Weidemann, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, the distinction between action selection and response vigour therefore provides the primary framework for characterising the influence of instrumental effort history.

Outcome-mediated accounts propose that during transfer, a Pavlovian cue reactivates its predicted outcome, which in turn provides access to instrumental information associated with that outcome (Cartoni et al., 2016; Holmes et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Outcome-mediated accounts propose that during transfer, a Pavlovian cue reactivates its predicted outcome, which in turn provides access to instrumental information associated with that outcome <ref type="bibr">(Cartoni et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Holmes et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Most PIT research has focused on outcome identity and value.

Here, we extend this logic to instrumental acquisition history, asking whether obtaining an outcome under relatively low-or high-effort requirements subsequently changes how a cue predicting that outcome influences behaviour.
Critically, the cue is never paired with either the instrumental action or its effort requirement.
The shared outcome provides the experimentally established link between the two learning phases.

If cues predicting outcomes previously obtained through high versus low effort subsequently elicit different behaviour, this would indicate that some feature of earlier instrumental acquisition history remains behaviourally relevant when the outcome is later predicted.

Such an effect would be consistent with instrumental history influencing behaviour indirectly through the shared outcome, although behavioural transfer cannot establish its precise representational format or retrieval mechanism.
Existing evidence also renders it plausible that such information could influence subsequent action.
Reward and effort jointly influence action preparation, and effortrelated value can modulate motor excitability even in the absence of value-based choice (Verguts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Reward and effort jointly influence action preparation, and effortrelated value can modulate motor excitability even in the absence of value-based choice <ref type="bibr">(Verguts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Neural evidence from PIT further shows that outcomepredictive cues can modulate premotor activity before instrumental choice and that instrumental R-O learning can alter subsequent processing of the same Pavlovian cues within premotor and broader action-related systems even when overt responding is unavailable (Finotti et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Neural evidence from PIT further shows that outcomepredictive cues can modulate premotor activity before instrumental choice and that instrumental R-O learning can alter subsequent processing of the same Pavlovian cues within premotor and broader action-related systems even when overt responding is unavailable <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Finotti et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Huang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, information acquired during instrumental learning may remain relevant to action-related processing when the associated outcome is later predicted by a Pavlovian cue.
Where would an effect of effort history be expressed?

The distinction between action selection and response vigour leads to a more specific question: does instrumental effort history change which action a cue promotes, how vigorously it promotes responding, or both?

An effect on response vigour would appear as a difference in overall responding to cues associated with high-versus low-effort outcomes without necessarily changing how responses are allocated between actions.
An effect on action selection, by contrast, would change the relative preference for the outcome-congruent over the incongruent response.
The direction of an effect on vigour is theoretically ambiguous.
From a prospectivecost perspective, an instrumental history associated with high effort might retain a costrelated influence and suppress subsequent responding.

High-effort options are generally avoided relative to otherwise equivalent low-effort alternatives unless increased reward compensates for their greater cost, and adaptive effort-investment accounts similarly propose that mobilisation depends on whether expected benefits justify anticipated demand (Chong et al., 2017; Escobar & Mitchell, 2025; Silvestrini et al., 2023; Vassena et al., 2019; Verguts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: High-effort options are generally avoided relative to otherwise equivalent low-effort alternatives unless increased reward compensates for their greater cost, and adaptive effort-investment accounts similarly propose that mobilisation depends on whether expected benefits justify anticipated demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Escobar & Mitchell, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Silvestrini et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Vassena et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verguts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Cues linked indirectly with highrequirement acquisition might therefore elicit less responding.

Conversely, retrospective-effort accounts suggest that successfully completed effort can enhance subsequent valuation, alter learning from rewarding outcomes, or increase willingness to mobilise effort again (Harmon-Jones et al., 2024; Inzlicht et al., 2018; Jarvis et al., 2022; Marcowski et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Conversely, retrospective-effort accounts suggest that successfully completed effort can enhance subsequent valuation, alter learning from rewarding outcomes, or increase willingness to mobilise effort again <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Harmon-Jones et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jarvis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Marcowski et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If such consequences remain associated with the instrumental history of an outcome, cues predicting outcomes obtained under higheffort requirements could instead elicit greater response vigour.
We therefore treated the direction of this effect as an open question.
For action selection, the question is whether instrumental history changes the strength of outcome-specific response bias.

If acquisition under different effort requirements alters how strongly a predicted outcome favours its corresponding action, the difference between congruent and incongruent responding should vary between high-and low-effort conditions.
If its influence is expressed primarily in vigour, overall response output may differ while relative response allocation remains comparatively stable.
Initial action choice provides a complementary measure of selection that is less influenced by repeated responding within a trial.
Across two experiments (Fig. 1), we examined whether physical effort experienced during instrumental learning subsequently shaped cue-guided behaviour.
text.formatted: Across two experiments (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), we examined whether physical effort experienced during instrumental learning subsequently shaped cue-guided behaviour.

text.text: Participants obtained different food outcomes through relatively low-or high-effort keypress requirements.
In a separate Pavlovian phase, distinct cues predicted those same outcomes but were never paired with the instrumental actions or effort requirements.
Transfer was then tested under extinction, with neither outcome delivery nor the original effort requirements present.
We assessed two expressions of transfer.
First, we tested whether cues predicting outcomes associated with high-effort acquisition elicited greater or lower response vigour than cues associated with low-effort acquisition.
Because prospective cost and retrospective-effort accounts imply opposing effects, the direction was treated as an open question.
Second, we tested whether acquisition history altered specific PIT, indexed by preferential responding towards the action associated with the cuepredicted outcome.
If instrumental effort history changes outcome-specific action selection, the magnitude of specific PIT should differ between effort conditions.
Alternatively, if its influence is expressed primarily in response vigour, overall response output should vary while relative response allocation and initial action selection remain stable.
These questions were tested first in a controlled laboratory experiment and then in an independent online experiment.

By separating instrumental effort from Pavlovian learning and from the demands present at transfer, the study tests whether features of prior instrumental acquisition history continue to influence cue-guided behaviour after the original effort requirement is no longer present, and whether that influence is expressed in response vigour, action selection, or both.
Experiments 1 and 2 used the same experimental design and identical task procedure but differed in testing context.
Experiment 1 was conducted in the laboratory, whereas Experiment 2 was administered online.
Experiment 1 was conducted in a multicomputer laboratory, with a maximum of six participants tested concurrently in each session.
To standardise instruction across participants and minimise differences between the laboratory and online experiments, the experimenter did not provide additional verbal task instructions.
Participants instead read all instructions on screen and were required to answer comprehension questions correctly before continuing.
Participants wore headphones to minimise interference from other participants in the testing room.
Experiment 2 followed the same procedure online.
Participants completed the experiment independently on a desktop or laptop computer at a time and location of their choosing and were instructed to perform the task alone in a quiet environment.
As in Experiment 1, progression through the relevant task phases required successful completion of the on-screen comprehension checks.
The research was conducted in accordance with the General Ethical Protocol of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at Ghent University.
All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the experiment and were informed that participation was restricted to individuals aged 16-35 years.
In Experiment 1, written informed consent was obtained using pen and paper before the testing session.
In Experiment 2, participants provided electronic informed consent by selecting an "I agree" option before beginning the online experiment.
The experiments were not preregistered.
Anonymised data, analysis code, and experimental materials is publicly available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23833767).
text.formatted: Anonymised data, analysis code, and experimental materials is publicly available on Zenodo (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23833767">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23833767</ref>).

text.text: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power (Version 3.1.9.6; Faul et al., 2009) for the critical Response × Cue interaction in a 2 × 5 repeated-measures ANOVA.
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power (Version 3.1.9.6; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Faul et al., 2009)</ref> for the critical Response × Cue interaction in a 2 × 5 repeated-measures ANOVA.

text.text: Both factors were manipulated within participants, comprising two instrumental responses (left vs. right) and five Pavlovian cues (CS1, CS2, CS3, CS4, and CS-).

Assuming an effect size of f = 0.20, an alpha level of 0.05, 80% power, a correlation of 0.50 among repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 0.75, the analysis indicated a minimum required sample of 38 participants.

The Response × Cue interaction was selected because the primary outcome-specific transfer hypothesis concerned whether Pavlovian cue identity differentially biased response allocation between the left and right instrumental actions.
A total of 57 participants were recruited through the Ghent University SONA participant pool and received one course credit per hour of participation.
One participant withdrew from the study.
Two participants were excluded because they did not meet the learning criteria described in the Exclusion criteria section, resulting in a final sample of 54 participants.
Participants were aged 17-25 years (M = 18.70, SD = 1.37; female = 40).
Handedness was predominantly right-sided: 47 participants (87.0%) were righthanded, 4 (7.4%) mixed-handed, and 3 (5.6%) left-handed.
A separate sample of 78 participants was recruited through the Ghent University SONA participant pool and received one course credit per hour of participation.
Eleven participants were excluded because they did not meet the learning criteria, resulting in a final sample of 67 participants.
Participants were aged 18-32 years (M = 19.75, SD = 2.34; female = 41).
Among the 65 participants with available handedness data, 51 (78.5%) were right-handed, 11 (16.9%) mixed-handed, and 3 (4.6%) left-handed.
The experiment was programmed in JavaScript using jsPsych (Version 7.2.1; de Leeuw, 2015) and run in Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge.
text.formatted: The experiment was programmed in JavaScript using jsPsych (Version 7.2.1; de <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Leeuw, 2015)</ref> and run in Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge.

text.text: To ensure that all task elements were displayed appropriately, the online experiment could only be initiated when the available display area was at least 1200 pixels wide and 750 pixels high.
Forty food images served as candidate reward outcomes during the initial foodselection procedure.
Based on participants' subjective wanting ratings, four foods were selected individually for each participant and randomly assigned to four outcome identities (O1-O4).
Five coloured cues served as Pavlovian conditioned stimuli (CSs).
Four cues (CS1-CS4) predicted the four food outcomes, whereas a fifth cue (CS-) served as a control stimulus and predicted no food outcome.
The assignment of colours to cue identities was randomised independently for each participant.

text.text: Instructions and comprehension questions were repeated until all questions had been answered correctly.
Participants first rated 40 food images presented individually in randomised order.

For each image, they indicated how much they wanted to eat the depicted food at that moment using a slider ranging from -10 (not at all) to +10 (very much), with the cursor initially positioned at zero.
Participants were required to move the slider before the continue button became available, preventing trials from being completed without an active response.
Trials were self-paced.
The program subsequently evaluated all possible combinations of four food images.
For each participant, the combination with the highest mean wanting rating was selected.
When multiple combinations had the same mean, the combination with the smallest standard deviation was selected, followed, if necessary, by the combination with the smallest rating range.
This procedure was designed to identify four highly wanted foods with relatively similar initial ratings.
The four selected foods were then randomly assigned to outcome identities O1-O4.

Following previous physical-effort paradigms in which effort requirements were individually calibrated (Arulpragasam et al., 2018; Gabay et al., 2024; Seaman et al., 2018), participants completed a pressing-capacity calibration to account for individual differences in motor response capacity.
text.formatted: Following previous physical-effort paradigms in which effort requirements were individually calibrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Arulpragasam et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Gabay et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Seaman et al., 2018)</ref>, participants completed a pressing-capacity calibration to account for individual differences in motor response capacity.

text.text: Participants completed 12 maximum pressing capacity (MPC) trials: six using the A key with the left index finger and six using the L key with the right index finger.
Trial order was randomised.
Each trial began with a slot machine displayed without response buttons for 1,000-1,500 ms.
The two response buttons, progress bars, and an instruction indicating which key to press were then displayed.
Participants were instructed to press the indicated key as many times as possible for 6 seconds.
The 6-s calibration interval began with the first valid keypress, ensuring an equivalent period of active responding across participants.
Pressing capacity was calculated separately for the left and right response sides.
For each side, the highest number of presses recorded across the six calibration trials was defined as the participant's MPC.
Low-and high-effort requirements were subsequently set to 20% and 80% of the corresponding side-specific MPC, respectively.
Thresholds were rounded to the nearest whole number and constrained to a minimum of one press.
This procedure yielded four instrumental response-effort conditions: left-low effort, left-high effort, right-low effort, and right-high effort (see Table 1).

Pavlovian training established one-to-one associations between four coloured cues (CS1-CS4) and the four food outcomes (O1-O4).
A fifth cue (CS-) served as a control stimulus and predicted no food outcome.
Cue colours were randomly assigned to cue identities for each participant.
As shown in Fig. 1c, each trial began with an unlit slot machine without buttons presented for 500-1,000 ms.

text.text: A coloured cue was then displayed for 2,000 ms, after which the cue remained on screen while either its associated food outcome or a nofood symbol was presented for an additional 1,000 ms.
Training comprised three blocks of 50 trials, yielding 150 trials in total.
Within each block, each of the five cues was presented 10 times in randomised order.

Each food-predictive cue (CS1-CS4) was followed by its corresponding food outcome on eight of the 10 presentations and by the no-food outcome on the remaining two presentations, corresponding to an 80% reinforcement probability.
CS-was followed by the no-food outcome on all presentations.
To monitor engagement during training, attention checks were included after randomly selected sequences of five to eight Pavlovian trials.
A red fixation cross appeared, and participants were required to press the space bar to continue.
Because the interval between checks was randomised, the total number of attention checks varied across participants.
At the end of each block, participants completed five selfpaced contingency questions assessing knowledge of the cue-outcome associations.
For each cue, they selected the outcome they believed was most likely to follow it from the four food images and the no-food symbol.
All participants completed all three Pavlovian-training blocks; progression through training did not depend on contingencyquestion accuracy.
Participants again rated their current hunger and completed the same five ratings for each of the four selected foods as at T0.
The transfer test assessed the influence of Pavlovian cues on freely chosen instrumental responding.
It comprised six blocks of 15 trials, yielding 90 trials in total.
Within each block, each of the five Pavlovian cues was presented three times in randomised order, resulting in 18 presentations of each cue across the transfer phase.
As shown in Fig. 1d, each trial began with an unlit slot machine without buttons presented for 1,000-1,500 ms.

text.text: The Pavlovian cue and both response buttons were then displayed simultaneously.
Participants were free to respond using the A key, the L key, or to alternate between the two responses; simultaneous keypresses were not permitted.
The first valid A or L keypress initiated a fixed 6-s response interval during which all subsequent keypresses and key releases were recorded.
No responseinitiation deadline was imposed during transfer; therefore, the trial remained on screen until a valid response was made.
No food outcomes were displayed during the transfer test.

Participants were nevertheless instructed that their responses could still earn food rewards and no actual food reward in the current studies, such that transfer was assessed under nominal extinction, consistent with common procedures in human PIT research (Badioli et al., 2024; Finotti et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026).

text.text: Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs were conducted on the same participantlevel datasets as the corresponding frequentist analyses, with participant included as a random factor.
For one-factor analyses, BF₁₀ compared the model containing the effect of interest with the participant-only null model.
For factorial analyses, modelaveraged inclusion Bayes factors (BFinc) quantified evidence for including each main effect and interaction across matched models.
For main effects, matching excluded models containing interactions involving the focal effect; for interactions, comparisons were restricted to models containing the constituent main effects.
Accordingly, BFinc > 1 favours inclusion of the effect, whereas BFinc < 1 favours its exclusion.
text.formatted: Accordingly, BFinc > 1 favours inclusion of the effect, whereas BFinc < 1 favours its exclusion.

text.text: Reward ratings were examined separately for each rating dimension using Time × Outcome repeated-measures ANOVAs.

Objective effort requirements were analysed using Response Side × Effort repeated-measures ANOVAs, and subjective effort ratings were compared across the four outcomes using within-participant ANOVAs.
Pavlovian and instrumental acquisition and post-task strategy reports were summarized descriptively.

Post-task motivation and contingency-belief ratings were tested against the scale midpoint using one-sided tests of whether ratings exceeded the midpoint and were compared between experiments using Mann-Whitney U tests.
Participant-level exclusions were based on acquisition of the instrumental and Pavlovian contingencies.
For instrumental learning, participants were required to achieve at least 50% response-side accuracy in their final completed training block.

For Pavlovian learning, participants were excluded if attention-check accuracy was below 50%, mean attention-check response time exceeded 5,000 ms, or cue-outcome contingency accuracy was below 50% in the final training block.
These criteria excluded 2 of 56 participants from Experiment 1 and 11 of 78 participants from Experiment 2, yielding final samples of 54 and 67 participants, respectively.
Subjective differentiation of the low-and high-effort contingencies was not used as an exclusion criterion.

Instead, sensitivity analyses repeated the primary transfer analyses in participants who correctly differentiated both effort contingencies in their final completed instrumental-training block (see Supplementary Results S2).

text.text: At the individual level, correct subjective differentiation of both effort contingencies increased descriptively across training.
Based on each participant's final completed block, both contingencies were correctly differentiated by 45 of 54 participants (83.3%) in Experiment 1 and 43 of 67 participants (64.2%) in Experiment 2.
Sensitivity analyses restricted to these participants are summarised in Section 3.8 and reported fully in Supplementary Results S2.
Participants successfully acquired the Pavlovian cue-outcome contingencies.

In Experiment 1, mean contingency accuracy was already high in the first training block and approached ceiling thereafter (Block 1: M = 94.1%, SD = 18.1%; Block 2: M = 98.9%, SD = 4.6%; Block 3: M = 99.6%, SD = 2.7%), with high accuracy across training overall (M = 97.5%, SD = 6.3%).

In Experiment 2, accuracy increased markedly across training (Block 1: M = 71.9%, SD = 34.3%; Block 2: M = 96.1%, SD = 11.1%; Block 3: M = 97.9%, SD = 7.9%), yielding an overall mean accuracy of 88.7% (SD = 14.7%).
Instrumental response-outcome knowledge showed a similar improvement across completed blocks.

Block 2 (M = 79.9%, SD = 26.6%); among participants who completed a third block, accuracy was 86.5% (SD = 21.0%).
Overall participant-level accuracy was 76.5% (SD = 19.0%), and final-block accuracy was 87.3% (SD = 20.6%).
Four participants completed training after two blocks, whereas 63 completed a third block.
Overall, contingency knowledge was high by the end of training in both experiments, although acquisition was more gradual in the online sample.

Across both experiments, therefore, reward-predictive cues increased instrumental responding relative to the control cue, and this effect was consistently larger for cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under high-effort requirements.

Having established a robust effect of effort history on overall response vigour, we next tested whether effort history also altered the relative allocation of responding between outcome-congruent and incongruent actions.
The primary analysis therefore examined whether the congruency effect (e.g., the difference between congruent and incongruent responding) varied between low-and high-effort conditions.
Participants made substantially more congruent than incongruent responses (Fig. 3a), providing strong evidence of specific PIT (F(1, 53) = 125.72, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.703; BFinc = 1.00 × 10 44 ).

text.text: The congruency effect was larger for high-than low-effort cues (difference = 4.76 responses; t(53) = 2.76, p = 0.008).
This difference reflected greater congruent responding under high effort (pBonf = 0.001), whereas incongruent responding did not differ between effort conditions (pBonf = 0.984).
Thus, Experiment 1 provided frequentist evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified the magnitude of specific PIT, but the Bayesian evidence for this modulation was weak.
The result therefore suggests an effort-related enhancement of the congruency effect without providing strong convergent evidence for it.

text.text: The descriptive pattern nevertheless resembled Experiment 1: the congruency effect was larger under highthan low-effort cues, although the difference was smaller and did not meet the conventional significance threshold.

To characterise the descriptive pattern, exploratory comparisons showed greater congruent responding under high-than loweffort cues (pBonf = 0.010), whereas incongruent responding did not differ between effort conditions (pBonf = 1.000).
Because the overall Congruency × Effort interaction was not reliable, however, these comparisons should be interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence that effort strengthened specific PIT.

Across both experiments, specific PIT was therefore robust, and the descriptive direction of the effort-related modulation was similar: high-effort cues produced a larger congruency difference, driven primarily by greater congruent responding.
However, this modulation was statistically reliable only in Experiment 1, Bayesian support was weak there, and Experiment 2 provided evidence favouring exclusion of the interaction.
The data therefore provide suggestive but inconclusive evidence that instrumental effort history amplified the magnitude of specific PIT.

text.text: The Bayes factors therefore favoured the model without an effect of effort history on initial action selection in both experiments.

Thus, cue-predicted outcomes reliably guided which action participants selected, but this initial selection was unaffected by whether the outcome had previously been obtained under low-or high-effort requirements.

Together with the response-count analyses, these findings indicate that instrumental effort history influenced response vigour more clearly and consistently than initial outcome-specific action selection, while leaving open a weaker modulation of the magnitude of specific PIT (see Supplementary Results S1).

To test whether the transfer findings depended on subjective differentiation of the effort manipulation, we repeated the analyses in participants who correctly differentiated both effort contingencies in their final completed training block.
The overall pattern was preserved: high-effort cues continued to elicit greater response vigour, and specific PIT remained robust in both experiments.

Evidence for effort-related amplification of specific PIT remained suggestive but inconsistent across experiments, whereas effort did not reliably alter proportional congruent response allocation or initial action selection.
Full results are reported in Supplementary Results S2 and Fig. S1.

text.text: Across two experiments, Pavlovian cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under high-effort response requirements elicited greater response vigour than response-matched low-effort cues.
This pattern was observed in both the laboratory and online experiments, even though the Pavlovian cues were never directly paired with the response requirements themselves.
At the same time, specific PIT remained robust under both effort conditions.

There was also some evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified specific PIT: the Congruency × Effort interaction was significant in Experiment 1 and showed a smaller effect in the same direction in Experiment 2.
However, this modulation was not consistently supported across experiments or statistical approaches, and effort history did not alter initial outcome-congruent action selection in either experiment.

Thus, instrumental acquisition history associated with high-effort requirements influenced response vigour robustly, while its influence on outcome-specific action selection was weaker and less consistently expressed.

Our main finding was that cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under higheffort requirements elicited greater subsequent response vigour than cues predicting response-matched outcomes obtained under low-effort requirements.
This direction contrasts with what might be expected if prior effort operated only as a cost.

In prospective effort-based decisions, increasing the physical or cognitive work required for a reward generally reduces willingness to pursue it and discounts its subjective value (Białaszek et al., 2017; Chong et al., 2017; Inzlicht et al., 2018; Salamone & Correa, 2024).
text.formatted: In prospective effort-based decisions, increasing the physical or cognitive work required for a reward generally reduces willingness to pursue it and discounts its subjective value <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Białaszek et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Salamone & Correa, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the present experiments, however, the effort had already been completed and was no longer required during transfer.

The direction of the effect is consistent with evidence that the consequences associated with completed effort can differ from the prospective costs of anticipated effort (Cheval et al., 2025; Inzlicht et al., 2018; Stähler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The direction of the effect is consistent with evidence that the consequences associated with completed effort can differ from the prospective costs of anticipated effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheval et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Stähler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern is broadly consistent with the retrospective side of the effort paradox: although effort is typically avoided prospectively, completed effort can sometimes enhance the later motivational significance of its consequences (Inzlicht et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This pattern is broadly consistent with the retrospective side of the effort paradox: although effort is typically avoided prospectively, completed effort can sometimes enhance the later motivational significance of its consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Inzlicht et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies have found greater preference for stimuli following more effortful responses, potentially reflecting effort justification or within-trial contrast between the demanding action and its subsequent consequence (Alessandri et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2005; Zentall, 2013).
text.formatted: Previous studies have found greater preference for stimuli following more effortful responses, potentially reflecting effort justification or within-trial contrast between the demanding action and its subsequent consequence <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alessandri et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Klein et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Zentall, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this literature in two respects.
First, the effect was expressed in subsequent response vigour rather than direct preference.
Second, the cues eliciting this difference had never been paired with effort; they were related to the effort manipulation only indirectly through their predicted outcomes.
Thus, some feature of prior high-effort instrumental experience remained behaviourally relevant when behaviour was later elicited by a separately learned outcome-predictive cue.
Nevertheless, the findings should not be taken to indicate that prior effort uniformly enhances subsequent motivation.
Retrospective effects of effort vary across tasks and conditions.

For instance, Tsukamoto et al. (2017) found greater preference for stimuli following difficult tasks only when participants made a high proportion of incorrect responses, whereas Aridan & Schonberg (2021) observed no change in snack preferences after associating the items with different levels of grip effort.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Tsukamoto et al. (2017)</ref> found greater preference for stimuli following difficult tasks only when participants made a high proportion of incorrect responses, whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aridan & Schonberg (2021)</ref> observed no change in snack preferences after associating the items with different levels of grip effort.

text.text: Other research similarly indicates that the effects of effort on subsequent reward evaluation can vary depending on the experimental context such as evaluation timing and perceived control (Harmon-Jones et al., 2024; Marcowski et al., 2025; Wu & Zheng, 2023).
text.formatted: Other research similarly indicates that the effects of effort on subsequent reward evaluation can vary depending on the experimental context such as evaluation timing and perceived control <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Harmon-Jones et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Marcowski et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Wu & Zheng, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas these studies primarily examined how previously exerted effort influences subsequent reward evaluation or preference, the present experiments demonstrate that instrumental effort history can also influence later response vigour indirectly through Pavlovian cues predicting the same outcomes.

Although the generalisability of this effect across different task contexts remains to be established, its consistent expression across the laboratory and online experiments provides converging evidence that prior instrumental effort can enhance subsequent cue-guided behavioural activation, even when effort is no longer required.
Importantly, greater cue-evoked vigour should not be interpreted as evidence that high effort increased the explicit value of the food outcomes.
Although wanting, deliciousness, and pleasantness generally declined after training, none of the rating dimensions showed reliable main effects of Outcome or Time × Outcome interactions.
Outcomes obtained through high effort therefore showed no selective increase in liking, wanting, pleasantness, deliciousness, or arousal.

Whereas previous retrospectiveeffort studies have often assessed changes in preference or valuation (Alessandri et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2005; Marcowski et al., 2025), the present effect was expressed in later response output.
text.formatted: Whereas previous retrospectiveeffort studies have often assessed changes in preference or valuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alessandri et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Klein et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Marcowski et al., 2025)</ref>, the present effect was expressed in later response output.

text.text: The results therefore support the narrower conclusion that response vigour was modulated by instrumental effort history associated with the higheffort response requirements, without demonstrating either explicit outcome upvaluation or that effort itself was the uniquely responsible feature of acquisition history.
The influence of instrumental effort history on outcome-specific action selection was less consistent than its influence on response vigour.
Participants responded more on the action associated with the cue-predicted outcome under both effort conditions, demonstrating robust specific PIT.
There was nevertheless some indication that this outcome-specific response bias was amplified following high-effort acquisition.
In Experiment 1, the Congruency × Effort interaction was significant, with a larger difference between congruent and incongruent responding for high-than low-effort cues.
Experiment 2 showed a smaller effect in the same descriptive direction, but the interaction did not reach conventional significance.
Moreover, Bayesian evidence for the interaction was weak in Experiment 1 and favoured its exclusion in Experiment 2.

The two experiments therefore provide suggestive, but not conclusive, evidence that instrumental effort history may have amplified the response-count congruency effect, rather than consistently strengthening relative outcome-specific action selection.
The form of this pattern is informative.
In both experiments, high-effort cues were associated primarily with greater congruent responding, whereas incongruent responding remained largely unchanged.
Thus, additional responding elicited by higheffort cues tended to occur on the action already favoured by the cue-predicted outcome.

However, a larger congruent-incongruent difference in response counts does not necessarily imply a stronger change in relative action selection, because response counts are also sensitive to overall response vigour.

Given that high-effort cues reliably increased total response output, greater vigour could amplify responding on the already preferred congruent action without substantially changing the relative bias between competing actions.
The initial-choice results support this more cautious interpretation.

Participants were more likely than chance to select the outcome-congruent action first under both low-and high-effort cues, but effort history did not alter the probability of making that congruent first choice in either experiment.
Bayesian evidence likewise favoured the model without an effort effect on initial action selection, although the strength of this evidence was modest.
Taken together, the results therefore do not support a simple conclusion that effort history either did or did not affect specific PIT.

Rather, high-effort acquisition may have amplified the behavioural expression of an existing outcomespecific response tendency, while evidence that it changed the underlying relative preference between actions was considerably weaker.
This pattern reinforces an empirical distinction between action selection and response vigour.

Pavlovian cues can bias which instrumental action is selected while also changing how strongly responding is expressed, and these effects need not vary together (Cartoni et al., 2016; Holmes et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Pavlovian cues can bias which instrumental action is selected while also changing how strongly responding is expressed, and these effects need not vary together <ref type="bibr">(Cartoni et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Holmes et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Specific PIT primarily indexes outcome-specific action selection, whereas general PIT primarily indexes response invigoration; neither form is defined exclusively by one behavioural dimension. Sennwald et al. (2020), for example, observed both outcome-specific transfer and broader increases in effort mobilization, whereas Lingawi et al. (2022) found that sensory-specific satiety abolished general invigoration while sparing specific PIT.
