(2020)</ref>, for example, observed both outcome-specific transfer and broader increases in effort mobilization, whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lingawi et al. (2022)</ref> found that sensory-specific satiety abolished general invigoration while sparing specific PIT.

text.text: General PIT can likewise occur without outcome-specific transfer (Degni et al., 2022), although specific PIT can be sensitive to outcome value under some conditions (Eder & Dignath, 2016; Seabrooke et al., 2017 Seabrooke et al., , 2019)).
text.formatted: General PIT can likewise occur without outcome-specific transfer <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Degni et al., 2022)</ref>, although specific PIT can be sensitive to outcome value under some conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Eder & Dignath, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Seabrooke et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Seabrooke et al., , 2019))</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this dissociation by showing that a feature of prior instrumental experience can influence cue-evoked vigour more consistently than the relative outcome-specific allocation of responding or the action selected first.

In motivational terms, this pattern broadly corresponds to stronger modulation of activational than directional aspects of motivation (Salamone & Correa, 2012 , 2024), without implying that these constructs are identical to response vigour and action selection.
text.formatted: In motivational terms, this pattern broadly corresponds to stronger modulation of activational than directional aspects of motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Salamone & Correa, 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>, without implying that these constructs are identical to response vigour and action selection.

text.text: Importantly, the evidence does not exclude a more modest influence on outcome-specific action selection; rather, such an influence was less consistently supported across experiments and measures than the effect on overall response output.

Similarly, although reward-predictive cues increased total responding relative to CS-, this comparison should not be interpreted as a pure measure of general PIT because all reward-predictive outcomes were also associated with instrumental actions.
The most distinctive feature of the present findings is that the effect of effort emerged across separately acquired instrumental and Pavlovian relations.

Effort was manipulated while participants learned the response-outcome contingencies, whereas the Pavlovian cues were subsequently paired with the same outcomes in the absence of any action or effort requirement.
During transfer, neither the outcomes nor the original effort requirements were presented.
The greater vigour elicited by high-effort outcome cues therefore cannot be attributed to direct cue-effort learning.
At the same time, the design does not establish that effort itself was retrieved when the Pavlovian cue was encountered.
High-effort requirements also involved greater motor repetition and a longer response sequence preceding each outcome.
The result therefore identifies behavioural relevance of instrumental acquisition history, rather than the specific feature of that history responsible for the effect.

This result is consistent with the central logic of PIT, according to which a predicted outcome connects independently acquired cue-outcome and response-outcome relations (Badioli et al., 2024; Cartoni et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This result is consistent with the central logic of PIT, according to which a predicted outcome connects independently acquired cue-outcome and response-outcome relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Badioli et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cartoni et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Forward cue-outcome relations support specific PIT, and transfer can vary with outcome value and expected outcome availability under particular testing conditions (Alarcón et al., 2018; Mahlberg et al., 2021; Seabrooke et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Forward cue-outcome relations support specific PIT, and transfer can vary with outcome value and expected outcome availability under particular testing conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alarcón et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Mahlberg et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Seabrooke et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Neural evidence further indicates learning-dependent differentiation in premotor and broader action-related systems during processing of outcome-predictive cues, including when overt responding is unavailable (Finotti et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Neural evidence further indicates learning-dependent differentiation in premotor and broader action-related systems during processing of outcome-predictive cues, including when overt responding is unavailable <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Finotti et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Huang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this account by showing that the vigour of behaviour elicited by an outcome-predictive cue can also vary according to the instrumental acquisition history associated with that outcome.

The suggestive modulation of the specific-PIT congruency effect further raises the possibility that acquisition history may influence not only overall response output but, more modestly, the expression of outcome-specific response tendencies.
However, the present evidence is not sufficiently consistent to establish this second effect.
The present pattern is therefore consistent with some feature of instrumental acquisition history remaining behaviourally relevant when the shared outcome was later predicted by a Pavlovian cue.

This extends the usual PIT question beyond which outcome and action are retrieved to whether characteristics of the instrumental history associated with that outcome can influence the later expression of cue-guided behaviour.
It does not, however, establish that those properties were encoded as discrete features of the outcome representation.
Effort-learning research provides a possible framework for understanding how such information could be acquired.

People can learn expected effort through predictionerror updating, and effort expectations can be integrated with reward information and ongoing sensorimotor feedback (Bi et al., 2026; Hauser et al., 2017; Skvortsova et al., 2014).
text.formatted: People can learn expected effort through predictionerror updating, and effort expectations can be integrated with reward information and ongoing sensorimotor feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bi et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hauser et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Skvortsova et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Repeated experience with stable low-and high-effort contingencies may therefore have established distinct expectations about the demands associated with obtaining each outcome.
One possibility is that learned expectations about effort demand became associated with the outcomes and were later made behaviourally relevant through the shared predicted outcome.

Such an account would provide one mechanism by which separately learned Pavlovian cues could gain access to information established during instrumental acquisition without requiring a direct cueeffort association.

This interpretation remains provisional, however, because the present experiments did not estimate effort expectations trial by trial, model effort prediction errors, or manipulate uncertainty during effort learning.

The results therefore show that some feature of instrumental acquisition history associated with high-effort response requirements remained behaviourally relevant during later cue-guided responding, but they do not establish that participants retrieved an explicit or computationally defined effort representation.
Several limitations qualify the interpretation of these findings.
First, the operationalisation of effort confounded experienced response demand with motor repetition and response-sequence length.

High-effort trials required 80% of participants' maximum pressing capacity, compared with 20% for low-effort trials, and therefore involved substantially more keypresses before the outcome was reached.

Although the block-completion criterion equated the target number of rewarded outcomes across response-effort conditions, high-effort response requirements involved substantially more repeated responding within each response-outcome episode.

Repetitive finger movements can induce central motor fatigue and perceived fatigue and can slow subsequent responding (Arias et al., 2015; Soto-Leon et al., 2020), while accumulating fatigue can also influence subsequent motivation and effort-based choice (Matthews et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Repetitive finger movements can induce central motor fatigue and perceived fatigue and can slow subsequent responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arias et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Soto-Leon et al., 2020)</ref>, while accumulating fatigue can also influence subsequent motivation and effort-based choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Matthews et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Motor repetition and its associated fatigue may therefore have contributed to the later cue effect independently of experienced effort.
Accordingly, the present findings should be attributed to instrumental acquisition history associated with the high-effort response requirement rather than to effort alone.
Future studies should hold response frequency constant while manipulating physical demand through force or resistance.

The effort contingencies were also stable and deterministic; manipulating average effort independently of noise or volatility would clarify whether cue-evoked vigour reflects expected demand, uncertainty about that demand, or both (Bi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The effort contingencies were also stable and deterministic; manipulating average effort independently of noise or volatility would clarify whether cue-evoked vigour reflects expected demand, uncertainty about that demand, or both <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Second, subjective differentiation of the effort contingencies was incomplete, particularly in Experiment 2.

Nevertheless, analyses restricted to participants who correctly differentiated the high-and low-effort outcomes reproduced the main pattern: More broadly, the findings connect two aspects of effort that are often studied separately.

Effort-based choice research primarily examines whether anticipated costs discourage action, whereas research on the effort paradox examines how completed effort shapes later evaluation (Chong et al., 2017; Inzlicht et al., 2018; Marcowski et al., 2025; Salamone & Correa, 2024; Wu & Zheng, 2023).
text.formatted: Effort-based choice research primarily examines whether anticipated costs discourage action, whereas research on the effort paradox examines how completed effort shapes later evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Marcowski et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Salamone & Correa, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Wu & Zheng, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present results show that instrumental effort history can remain behaviourally relevant when the corresponding outcomes are later signalled by separately learned cues.
This influence was expressed most clearly and consistently in response vigour.
There was also suggestive evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified the magnitude of specific PIT, but this effect was weaker and less consistent across experiments and measures.
Thus, prior instrumental history appears to influence how strongly cue-guided behaviour is expressed more robustly than it alters which action is selected.

Across two experiments, Pavlovian cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under high-effort response requirements elicited greater subsequent response vigour than response-matched low-effort cues, despite never being directly paired with those requirements.
Specific PIT remained robust under both effort conditions, and there was suggestive evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified its magnitude, particularly in response counts.
However, the Congruency × Effort interaction was significant only in
Experiment 1, with Bayesian evidence varying in strength across analyses, and no reliable effort-related difference in initial outcome-congruent action selection was observed in either experiment.
Instrumental acquisition history associated with higheffort response requirements was therefore expressed more clearly and consistently in response vigour than in relative action selection.

These findings show that features of prior effortful instrumental experience can remain behaviourally relevant when the corresponding outcomes are later signalled by separately learned environmental cues, while leaving open whether that history also produces a smaller modulation of outcome-specific action selection.

To examine whether the transfer findings depended on participants' subjective differentiation of the effort manipulation, the principal transfer analyses were repeated among participants whose subjective effort ratings in their final completed instrumental-training block correctly differentiated both effort contingencies.

Because these analyses were conducted in reduced subsamples selected on the basis of subjective effort ratings, they were treated as sensitivity analyses rather than replacements for the full-sample analyses.

High-effort cues elicited more responding than low-effort cues (pBonf = 0.002), and both low-effort (pBonf = 0.001) and high-effort cues (pBonf < 0.001) elicited more responding than the control cue.

Specific PIT was robust under both low-effort cues (Congruent: M = 25.2, SD = 8.10; Incongruent: M = 5.49, SD = 6.95; pBonf < 0.001) and high-effort cues (Congruent: M = 30.4, SD = 8.32; Incongruent: M = 4.67, SD = 6.15; pBonf < 0.001).

text.text: Congruent responding was greater under high than low effort (pBonf = 0.001), whereas incongruent responding did not differ between effort conditions (pBonf = 1.000).
Thus, within the Experiment 1 sensitivity sample, both the frequentist and Bayesian analyses supported a larger raw congruency effect under high-effort than low-effort cues.

Specific PIT also remained robust in Experiment 2, with main effects of Congruency (F(1, 42) = 81.10, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.659; BFinc = 3.61 × 10³ ¹ ) and Effort (F(1, 42) = 13.67, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.246; BFinc = 0.44).

Participants made substantially more congruent than incongruent responses under both low-effort cues (Congruent: M = 22.6, SD = 6.56; Incongruent: M = 6.34, SD = 6.17; pBonf < 0.001) and high-effort cues (Congruent: M = 25.1, SD = 9.08; Incongruent: M = 6.97, SD = 7.03; pBonf < 0.001).

text.text: Neither congruent (pBonf = 0.064) nor incongruent responding (pBonf = 0.935) differed significantly between effort conditions.
Thus, in Experiment 2, specific PIT remained robust, but both the frequentist and Bayesian analyses provided no reliable evidence that effort history altered the magnitude of the congruency effect.

The same pattern was observed in Experiment 2.

Congruent first-choice proportions were above chance under both low-effort (M = 0.755, SD = 0.177; pBonf < 0.001) and high-effort cues (M = 0.736, SD = 0.205; pBonf < 0.001), but did not differ between effort conditions (F(1, 42) = 1.12, p = 0.295, ηp² = 0.026; BF₁₀ = 0.36).

text.text: The Bayes factors therefore favoured the model without an Effort effect on initial action selection in both experiments, although the evidence was modest.

Thus, even among participants whose final-block ratings clearly differentiated the effort conditions, instrumental effort history did not reliably influence which outcome-specific action was selected first.

Overall, restricting the analyses to participants whose subjective effort ratings in their final completed training block differentiated both effort contingencies preserved the principal pattern observed in the full samples.
High-effort cues continued to elicit greater overall response vigour, while robust specific PIT was observed under both effort conditions.
Evidence that effort history modulated specific PIT nevertheless remained inconsistent across experiments.
In Experiment 1, the raw response-count analysis showed an Effort × Congruency interaction, with Bayesian evidence favouring inclusion of the interaction.
In Experiment 2, the interaction was not reliable and Bayesian evidence favoured its exclusion.
The sensitivity analyses therefore reinforce the overall conclusion that instrumental effort acquisition history influenced response vigour more consistently than outcome-specific action selection.

Note. (a) Overall procedure.

Both experiments comprised food selection, pressing-capacity calibration, baseline food ratings (T0), effort-based instrumental training, Pavlovian training, post-training food ratings (T1), the Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT) test, and a post-task questionnaire. (b) Effort instrumental training.
Participants repeatedly pressed the indicated response within 6 s to fill a response bar and obtain a food outcome.
Low -and high-effort requirements were individualized according to maximum pressing capacity (MPC). (c) Pavlovian training.
Participants passively observed coloured cues followed by their corresponding food outcomes, with no response available, thereby learning the cueoutcome associations. (d) Transfer test.
Each cue was presented while both responses were available, but no outcomes were delivered. (e) Contingency structure.
The left response produced O1 following low effort and O2 following high effort, whereas the right response produced O3 following low effort and O4 following high effort.
The Pavlovian contingencies were CS1-O1, CS2-O2, CS3-O3, and CS4-O4; CS-predicted no outcome.
Food outcomes were individually tailored during the experiments.

The task procedure was identical across experiments except for the mode of administration.
Before pressing-capacity calibration, instrumental effort training, Pavlovian training, and the transfer test, participants foods.
Each food was rated on five dimensions: (a) general liking, (b) current wanting, (c) perceived deliciousness, (d) perceived pleasantness, and (e) arousal.
Ratings were made on 7-point scales ranging from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much).
The slider was initially positioned at the midpoint of the scale, and participants were required to move it before continuing.
Trials were self-paced.

The order of the four food outcomes was randomised, whereas the five rating questions were presented in a fixed order within each food.2.5.4 Phase 4: Instrumental effort trainingInstrumental effort training established associations between two instrumental responses (left and right), two effort requirements (low and high), and four food outcomes (O1-O4).
Participants first completed four practice trials, one for each Response × Effort combination, presented in randomised order.

Practice trials followed the same response procedure as experimental trials but used a grey circle as the outcome and did not provide food rewards.As shown in Fig.1b, each trial began with a slot machine displayed without response buttons for 500-1,000 ms.
The response buttons, progress bars, and an instruction indicating the required response were then presented.
Participants repeatedly pressed either the A key with the left hand or the L key with the right hand to reach the corresponding effort threshold.
The 6-s response interval began with the first correct keypress.
Participants had up to 12 s from presentation of the response display to initiate responding; failure to do so resulted in "Too slow" feedback.
The same feedback was presented if responding was initiated but the required effort threshold was not reached within 6 s.
Feedback was displayed for 1,000 ms.When the required effort threshold was reached, the response buttons disappeared and the trial continued until completion of the 6-s response interval.

On valid trials, the food outcome associated with the corresponding Response x Effort condition was displayed with a probability of 75%; on the remaining 25% of valid trials, a grey circle indicating no reward was displayed.

Trials on which the effort threshold was not reached produced no food outcome and did not contribute to the block-completion criterion: the block ended when participants had obtained nine rewarded outcomes in each of the four response-effort conditions.

Because reward delivery was probabilistic and unsuccessful trials did not contribute to this criterion, the number of trials required to complete a block varied across participants.At the end of each block, participants completed eight contingency questions assessing knowledge of the instrumental contingencies.
For each food outcome, they indicated which response key was most likely to produce it and rated the effort required to obtain it on a scale from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high).

A block was classified as correct when participants identified O1 and O2 as associated with the left response and O3 and O4 as associated with the right response, and rated the high-effort outcome as requiring greater effort than the corresponding low-effort outcome on each response side (O2 > O1 and O4 > O3).

All analyses were conducted in R. Data processing and visualization used tidyverse and ggplot2, repeated-measures ANOVAs used afex, planned comparisons used emmeans, and Bayesian ANOVAs used BayesFactor, and inclusion Bayes factors were obtained using bayestestR.

Tests were twosided unless otherwise specified, with α = 0.05.
Planned comparisons were Bonferronicorrected within each family of contrasts and are denoted pBonf.
Overall response vigour was defined as the total number of left and right responses emitted during each cue.

Responses during CS1-CS4 were coded as congruent when the response had previously produced the outcome predicted by the cue and incongruent when it corresponded to the alternative response.
Mean response counts were analysed using a 2 (Effort: low, high) × 2 (Congruency: congruent, incongruent) repeated-measures ANOVA.
The main effect of Congruency indexed specific PIT, whereas the Congruency × Effort interaction tested whether instrumental effort history altered the relative outcome-specific response bias.
Planned comparisons tested congruent versus incongruent responding separately within each effort condition and low-versus high-effort responding separately for congruent and incongruent responses.

In Experiment 1, 33 participants (61.1%) reported an outcome-based strategy, 12 (22.2%) a non-outcome-based strategy, and 9 (16.7%) a mixed strategy.

In Experiment 2, among the 65 participants who provided post-task data, 32 (49.2%) reported an outcome-based strategy, 23 (35.4%) a non-outcome-based strategy, and 10 (15.4%) a mixed strategy; strategy and rating data were missing for two participants.In Experiment 1, motivation was significantly above the midpoint (M = 4.69, SD = 1.99; t(53) = 2.53, p = 0.007, Cohen's d = 0.35), whereas contingency beliefs did not differ from the midpoint (M = 4.04, SD = 1.80; t(53) = 0.15, p = 0.440, Cohen's d = 0.02).

In Experiment 2, neither motivation (M = 3.97, SD = 2.26; t(64) = -0.11, p = 0.543, Cohen's d = -0.01) nor contingency beliefs (M = 3.63, SD = 1.75; t(64) = -1.71, p = 0.953, Cohen's d = -0.21) were significantly above the midpoint.
Neither motivation (U = 2081.50, p = 0.078, rank-biserial r = -0.19) nor contingency beliefs (U = 1995.50, p = 0.194, rank-biserial r = -0.14) differed significantly between experiments.
high-effort cues elicited greater vigour, and specific PIT remained robust under both effort conditions.

The Effort × Congruency interaction was significant in Experiment 1, with Bayesian evidence favouring its inclusion, whereas the interaction was not significant in Experiment 2, with Bayesian evidence favouring its exclusion.
Effort did not reliably alter initial action selection in either experiment.

These sensitivity analyses therefore reinforced the robustness of the response-vigour effect while leaving the evidence for effort-related modulation of specific PIT inconsistent across experiments.Incomplete subjective differentiation therefore appears insufficient to explain the findings, although the present study cannot establish whether explicit knowledge of effort history was necessary.
The absence of effort-specific changes in food ratings also limits conclusions about outcome value.
Although explicit ratings may not capture every motivational consequence of effort, the present data provide no evidence that high-effort outcomes were consciously valued more positively.
Future studies could include direct-choice and outcome-devaluation measures.
An additional Pavlovian reward outcome without an instrumental association would also help distinguish general cue-evoked invigoration from effects that depend on the outcome's instrumental history.
Finally, replication across laboratory and online experiments strengthens the vigour effect, but generalizability remains limited by the repetitive keypress manipulation.
Replication using sustained force, resistance-based or cognitive effort, and more naturalistic effort histories is therefore needed.
